title: Interpreting algebraic notation
summary: Interpret coefficients, powers, products, brackets and fraction bars so that algebraic notation matches the intended operation order.
objectives: Identify terms, factors, coefficients, powers, numerators and denominators.
Translate verbal descriptions into unambiguous bracketed or fractional notation.
Distinguish expressions that look similar but have different structures.

blocks.text: An expression is built from terms separated by addition or subtraction. Each term may contain numerical and variable factors. In −4x²y, the coefficient is −4 and the variable factors are x² and y. The exponent 2 applies only to x; it means x multiplied by x. A missing multiplication sign between a number, letter or bracket is conventional algebraic notation.

Brackets make a group act as one quantity. Thus 3(x + y) means three copies of the entire sum, while 3x + y multiplies only x by 3. Read from the outermost operation inward: 3(x + y) says “three times the sum”, whereas (3x + y)/5 says “one fifth of the whole numerator”.

sections.title: Worked example: a squared quotient

prompt.text: Write the square of the quotient of a + b and 3c, then simplify the squared denominator.

content.text: Keep the sum a + b together and form the quotient.
Square the complete quotient with outer brackets.
Apply the square to numerator and denominator.

sections.verification_note: For any non-zero c, substituting values into the bracketed quotient before squaring gives the same result as the final fraction.

blocks.text: A fraction bar groups everything in its numerator and everything in its denominator. The expression (x + 7)/5 means add first and divide the result by 5. By contrast, x + 7/5 divides only 7 by 5. When typing, use brackets to reproduce the grouping shown by a printed fraction bar.

Powers also depend on grouping. In −p² the square applies to p before the negative sign, giving −(p²). In (−p)² the negative value is included in the base, so the result is positive. Careful brackets prevent sign errors during later substitution.

sections.title: Worked example: translate a layered phrase

prompt.text: Write twice the difference between p and 5, divided by q squared.

content.text: The difference between p and 5 is a grouped subtraction.
Twice that difference forms the complete numerator.
Divide by q squared, keeping the denominator intact.

sections.verification_note: With p = 9 and q = 2, the phrase gives twice 4 divided by 4, which is 2; the expression also gives 2.

blocks.text: A coefficient and an exponent perform different operations: 3x is three copies of x, while x³ is three factors of x. The expression ab means a multiplied by b, but a + b remains a sum. Never cancel terms across addition: the a in (a + b)/a cannot be cancelled because the numerator is not a single product.

To interpret unfamiliar notation, name the outermost operation, identify its complete inputs, and then move inward. Rewrite the expression with explicit multiplication signs and brackets if necessary. This process is slower than guessing from visual proximity and is far more reliable.

prompt.text: Write one fifth of the sum of x and 7 as an algebraic expression.

feedback.text: Keep x + 7 together in the numerator: (x + 7)/5.

blocks.text: Identify terms and factors, distinguish coefficients from powers, and treat brackets and fraction bars as grouping symbols. Translate phrases from the named group outward, add brackets when typing a fraction or power, and check that every multiplier or exponent acts on exactly the intended quantity.
